facts: I think I started using AI for programming about 6–12 months before the original interview.
I confirmed the second option for when I started using AI for programming, corresponding to my preceding estimate of 6–12 months.
At the original interview, my primary AI support for work was GitHub Copilot integrated into my IDE.
In addition to GitHub Copilot with IDE integration, I also use ChatGPT.
Yeah.
AI is always integrated directly into my IDE.
I use AI for almost everything in programming; for example, I often use it for debugging when I do not know where a bug originates. I also wrote this in the form.

I use AI to explain pieces of code and how parts of a module work together (the source transcribes the parts as 'multiple fires'). I also use AI for new features, but I am more critical of its output there. I use it to find things in our code base because it is huge and searching everything by myself is very difficult.
For the AI-use frequency table, I initially suggested often for all activities, with documentation sometimes; I specified further exceptions in my following answers.
I rated AI use for writing tests as very often and for explaining concepts or learning as sometimes, with a later qualification of sometimes or rarely for learning.
For explaining concepts or learning with AI, I was between sometimes and rarely.
Yeah.
My last work task was extending a component with two new color variants. I had a user story describing the requirement and a Figma design, which I checked.

For the component color-variant task, I opened Figma and examined the design myself. I talked to the designer and the business person who requested it to confirm what they wanted to achieve and explain the trade-offs, particularly that the requested color was not very accessible. Then I opened a new context in VS Code and dragged relevant folders into the Copilot chat context. I normally use the tool/model transcribed as 'cloud code', primarily version 4.5.
Although I normally use the model transcribed as cloud code 4.5, I know that 4.6 is the newer version.

I prefer version 4.5 because it feels faster; 4.6 seems slower and more in-depth, which I did not need for the color-variant task. After adding the relevant files, I explained the task and instructed the AI to iterate through a to-do list, waiting for my confirmation after each item. It completed all items without waiting, but I checked the files and found the changes acceptable.

For the new color variants, I disliked some parts of the AI implementation, including its Storybook story, and asked it to change them. I noticed that it had omitted the accessibility requirement: people using accessibility tools to read content should receive the accessible version, while the non-accessible version should be available to those who can see it.

The non-accessible color version was intended for those who can visualize it with their own eyes. I then created a pull request and requested review. As usual, a review can be approved or require more discussion; this one involved extra discussion.

After the pull request was approved, there was another comment. I asked AI to write Markdown documentation instead of doing it myself. It wrote too much, so I removed about 75% and kept about 25%, then merged the contribution into master.
I estimate that I spent two to three hours actively working on the entire component color-variant task, excluding the periods when I waited for review and did other work.

The color-variant task was not especially difficult technically; what was time-consuming was communicating with the relevant people, getting approval and ensuring they accepted the associated risks, trade-offs and compromises.
The component color-variant task arrived as a ticket, specifically a user story. My team includes designers and developers, and designers have their own section on our board.
Designers have their own Scrum process. When a design story reaches technical review, I as a developer create a story for myself, which the team estimates together during an estimation session.

After the technical story was estimated, someone had to pick it up. I picked it up myself, kept the relevant parts of the design user story in my developer user story and completed the task as described earlier.
I initially rated the first general programming activity as very often; later I confirmed that my writing-code rating was fine.
I rated testing as very often in the general programming-activity table.
I confirmed I was asking about the previous table where activities were rated from almost never to very often.
I initially understood the previous table as being about AI tools and was still clarifying what the new table measured.

I accepted the explanation of the two frequency tables but said the wording of the general activity question was confusing; it begins by describing researchers identifying common software-development activities.
On rereading the general programming-activity question, I could understand that it asked how often each listed activity comes up in my typical workday.

I found the wording 'how often does it come up' confusing because it made me wonder what comes up. After the clarification, I corrected my ratings: writing code remained as previously rated, very often, and reviewing code became very often.
In my corrected general programming-activity ratings, bug fixing and debugging are very often.
In my corrected general programming-activity ratings, testing or running tests and specification or working with requirements are both very often.
In my corrected general programming-activity ratings, documentation is rare.
In my corrected general programming-activity ratings, learning and continuous learning are often.
Yeah.
I clarified that I was selecting the activity that takes the most time overall.
Specification is the activity that takes up most of my time overall, out of writing code, reviewing code, bug fixing, testing and specifications.

As an example of specification work, our platform's profile settings have tabs and lists of settings. For instance, a login tab can contain login methods, opening a page with three login-method options that can be toggled on or off.

For the profile-settings task, the designers wanted a three-level nested mobile menu: a login-methods entry leads to categories such as username and password or social login, and social login leads to options such as Google or Apple. The existing framework was not very scalable for three-level settings nesting, so adding it was not straightforward. I made a proof of concept I thought was acceptable, but others disagreed and strongly favored a different approach. We had to align with them, wait f

For the nested-settings proof of concept, I used Copilot to explore ways of implementing it. It gave me two options, and I chose the one that made the most sense given our repository structure. I opened a pull request in Azure DevOps and communicated with the relevant people over Teams.
After the discussion over the nested-settings implementation, I returned to VS Code and implemented a different approach.
The tools I used for the nested-settings specification task included Azure DevOps, VS Code and Teams; I had also used Copilot for the proof of concept.
Aligning with the people involved in the nested-settings task took about 90% of the time.
I answered yes when asked whether I often need to work with code I did not write or unfamiliar parts of the code base; I then described an example of unfamiliar code.
The recent nested-settings feature is a good example of unfamiliar code: I had not worked in that part of the application before and needed to understand it to add the new feature.
To add the feature in the unfamiliar part of the application, I had to understand how that part was organized and how its original developers thought about it.
I used Copilot particularly to explore implementation options for the feature in the unfamiliar code, considering the patterns commonly used throughout our code base.
To ensure the unfamiliar-code change did not break anything, I relied on tests, manually testing it myself and having the change reviewed.

Our code base has many integration tests, roughly 10,000 by my estimate. On the first attempt at the change in that unfamiliar part of the repository, I saw roughly 20 tests fail, showing me that my change had broken another part of the application that should not have been affected.

My recent AI-assisted task was the same component color-variant and accessibility task described earlier. I told the AI what needed to be done, it implemented the changes, I iterated and opened a pull request.
Exactly that.

I used AI in the color-variant task after gathering all specifications and understanding what needed to be achieved; instead of writing the implementation myself, I asked AI to write the code and reviewed it.

For the progress bar component, I prompted AI to extend the color prop with two additional named color variants and specified their colors. I warned that the colors were not accessible and instructed it to fall back to accessible colors when the prop transcribed as 'area hidden' was present.
I also prompted AI to write a Storybook story for the progress-bar color variants and run TypeScript and ESLint to check that the code was correct and TypeScript did not fail.
In the progress-bar task, AI not only wrote the code but also ran scripts for me.

I verified the AI-generated progress-bar implementation by reading the code and clicking 'keep' on individual changes or the whole file if it made sense, opening Storybook and visually checking the added colors, and running TypeScript and ESLint to check semantics and types.
Oh, and that was it.
For the progress-bar task, the AI essentially performed the same work I would have done manually; I did not see it as changing the approach.
The AI did not provide a different way of implementing the progress-bar functionality from the approach I would have used.

Before using AI, I had added other components on earlier occasions. When I was relatively new to adding them, my implementation did not match the way colleagues had decided components should be written in our library. It took longer and was more cumbersome to learn the existing code-base patterns.

Building similar components without AI required more time, many reviews and addressing review comments. I think that time could have been shortened because AI can inspect other files to understand the existing patterns.

I now consider AI-assisted development stable enough that I generally start by asking AI to write the code rather than writing it manually; I review it, can discard what it wrote and prompt again for a different implementation. My work is more about iterating on AI-generated code than manually writing as much code. The source contains an unclear phrase 'I trust disregard what it wrote'; I do not infer unconditional trust from it.
I always validate AI output.
To validate AI output, I read it myself, understand what the AI did and decide whether it is what I would have done, whether the logic and approach are correct.
When reviewing AI-generated code, I also check whether it is cleanly written and whether the names of functions make sense to me as a human reader.
I validate AI-generated code logic myself and also rely on safety nets such as testing and other tooling.

I distinguish AI models, whose names were transcribed as Cloud Sonnet and Cloud Kitaki, from agentic coding. I understand agentic coding as models being capable of running tasks by themselves, understanding task context and iterating toward a high standard.
One tool for the agentic coding approach I was describing is called Open Code.
I named Open Code and another newer tool transcribed as cloud code as examples related to agentic coding.

I contrasted writing code in VS Code with Copilot reading repository context against Open Code, which I described as a robot-like tool to which plugins can be added, able to understand things at a broader contextual level.
I thought the interview could usefully ask whether developers have used agentic coding.
With the agentic coding approach I described, I would not need to approve every small AI change in VS Code because it can create an entire feature by itself.
Yes.

I think programming with AI and agentic coding is shifting developers toward being operators rather than the people directly creating things: tools such as the ones I called cloud code and Open Code can perform the work when we operate them.
I see a paradigm shift in developers' work from writing code manually toward operating AI coding tools.
I compared the shift from manual programming to AI-assisted programming to a woodworker switching from a manual saw to an electric saw.
In my electric-saw analogy for AI coding tools, the newer tool makes work cleaner and easier to execute than cutting wood manually.
I reaffirmed the manual-saw versus electric-saw analogy for the changing role of developers using AI tools.
That's it, yeah.
